title: Indian subcontinent
wiki_lead: The Indian subcontinent is a physiographic region of Asia encompassing most of the Himalayas and the land to their south, projecting into the Indian Ocean between the Bay of Bengal to the east and the Arabian Sea to the west. Politically, the Indian subcontinent is divided among Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, whose territories were part of historical and British India before its partition in 1947. Although the terms Indian subcontinent and South Asia are often used interchangeably to denote a wider region which includes, in addition, Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka, the Indian subcontinent term is more geophysical, whereas South Asia is more geopolitical.  South Asia is also frequently defined to include Afghanistan, which is not considered part of the subcontinent even in extended usage.
wiki_fulltext:
The Indian subcontinent is a physiographic region of Asia encompassing most of the Himalayas and the land to their south, projecting into the Indian Ocean between the Bay of Bengal to the east and the Arabian Sea to the west. Politically, the Indian subcontinent is divided among Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, whose territories were part of historical and British India before its partition in 1947. Although the terms Indian subcontinent and South Asia are often used interchangeably to denote a wider region which includes, in addition, Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka, the Indian subcontinent term is more geophysical, whereas South Asia is more geopolitical.  South Asia is also frequently defined to include Afghanistan, which is not considered part of the subcontinent even in extended usage.


Name
The region surrounding and southeast of the Indus River was often simply referred to as India in many historical sources. Even today, historians use India to denote the entire Indian subcontinent when discussing history up until the era of the British Raj. Over time, however, the term India evolved to refer to a distinct political entity that eventually became a nation-state.
According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the term subcontinent signifies a "subdivision of a continent which has a distinct geographical, political, or cultural identity" and also a "large land mass somewhat smaller than a continent". Its use to signify the Indian subcontinent is evidenced from the early twentieth century when most of the territory was either part of the British Empire or allied with them. It was a convenient term to refer to the region comprising both British India and the princely states.
The term has been particularly common in the British Empire and its successors, while the term South Asia is the more common usage in Europe and North America as well as in most countries in South Asia itself sometimes. According to historians Sugata Bose and Ayesha Jalal, the Indian subcontinent has come to be known as South Asia "in more recent and neutral parlance". Indologist Ronald B. Inden argues that the usage of the term South Asia is becoming more widespread since it clearly distinguishes the region from East Asia.
Since the Partition of British India, citizens of Pakistan (which became independent of British India in 1947) and Bangladesh (which became independent of Pakistan in 1971) often perceive the use of Indian subcontinent as offensive and suspicious because of the dominant placement of India in the term. As such it is being increasingly less used in those countries. Meanwhile, many Indian analysts prefer to use the term because of the socio-cultural commonalities of the region. The region has also been called the "Asian subcontinent", the "South Asian subcontinent", as well as "India" or "Greater India" in the classical and pre-modern sense.
The sport of cricket, introduced to the region by the British, is notably popular in India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. Within a cricket context, these countries are sometimes referred to simply as the subcontinent e.g. "Australia's tour of the subcontinent". The term is also sometimes used adjectivally in cricket e.g. "subcontinental conditions".


Geology

Before the Indian plate rifted from Gondwana and drifted northward toward Eurasia, two other landmasses, the Qiangtang terrane and Lhasa terrane, had accreted to Eurasia.  The Qiantang and Lhasa terranes were part of the string of microcontinents Cimmeria, today constituting parts of Turkey, Iran, Pakistan (including the Karakoram), China, Myanmar, Thailand and Malaysia, which closed the Paleo-Tethys Ocean to the north of them and opening the Neo-Tethys Ocean between them and Gondwana, eventually colliding with Eurasia, and creating the Cimmerian Orogeny.  
After the Lhasa terrane had adjoined Eurasia, an active continental margin opened along its southern flank, to the south of which the Neo-Tethys oceanic plate had begun to subduct. Magmatic activity along this flank produced the Gangdese batholith in what is today the Tibetan trans-Himalaya. Another subduction zone opened to the west, in the ocean basin above the Kohistan-Ladakh island arc. This island arc—formed by one oceanic plate subducting beneath another, its magma rising and creating continental crust—drifted north, closed its ocean basin and collided with Eurasia.  Ladakh is today in the Indian-administered region of Kashmir and Kohistan in the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan, both on the Indian subcontinent. 
The collision of India with Eurasia closed the Neo-Tethys Ocean. The suture zone (in this instance, the remnants of the Neo-Tethys subduction zone pinched between the two continental crusts), which marks India's welding to Eurasia, is called the Indus-Yarlung suture zone. It lies north of the Himalayas. The headwaters of the Indus River and the Yarlung Tsangpo (later in its course, the Brahmaputra) flow along this suture zone. These two Eurasian rivers, whose courses were continually diverted by the rising Himalayas, define the western and eastern limits, respectively, of the Himalayan mountain range.


Religion
grok_lead: The Indian subcontinent is a physiographical peninsula of southern Asia, encompassing the sovereign nations of India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, and the Maldives, defined by its separation from the rest of Eurasia by the Himalayas and the Hindu Kush mountain ranges. Geologically, it constitutes the northern portion of the Indian tectonic plate, which drifted northward from Gondwana and collided with the Eurasian Plate approximately 50 million years ago, uplifting the Himalayan range and shaping the region's dramatic topography including the Indo-Gangetic Plain, Deccan Plateau, and coastal lowlands. Covering roughly 4.4 million square kilometers, the subcontinent supports a combined population exceeding 1.9 billion as of 2024, representing nearly one-quarter of global humanity and resulting in some of the world's highest population densities, particularly in the fertile alluvial plains. This natural geographic expanse closely mirrors the ancient definition preserved in the Sanskrit text Vishnu Purana, which describes the landmass as the region situated north of the Indian Ocean and south of the snowy Himalayas. Historically, the region has been a cradle of ancient civilizations, including the northwest Indian subcontinental Indus Valley Civilization (c. 3300â1300 BCE)ârenowned for its sophisticated urban design, advanced drainage systems, and trade networks âand the heartland of Indo-Aryan Vedic culture (c. 1500â500 BCE), with foundational texts like the Rigveda (c. 1500â1200 BCE), and the birthplace of major world religions such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, fostering profound philosophical, mathematical, and architectural contributions that influenced global thought. Over millennia, empires like the Maurya, Gupta, and Mughal unified large swaths, driving advancements in science, trade, and governance, though interspersed with invasions, feudal fragmentation, and colonial exploitation under British rule from the 18th to 20th centuries, culminating in the 1947 partition that created India and Pakistan amid mass migrations and violence claiming over a million lives. In modern times, the subcontinent exhibits stark contrasts: India has emerged as a rapidly industrializing economy with strengths in information technology, pharmaceuticals, and space exploration, achieving GDP growth rates often above 7% annually, while grappling with poverty, inequality, and environmental degradation from overpopulation and urbanization. Pakistan and Bangladesh face challenges from political instability, frequent natural disasters like cyclones and floods, and Islamist militancy, yet contribute through textiles and remittances; smaller Himalayan states like Nepal and Bhutan emphasize hydropower and tourism amid vulnerability to seismic activity and climate change. Culturally diverse with over 2,000 ethnic groups, hundreds of languages, and syncretic traditions, the region contends with inter-communal tensions, notably Hindu-Muslim divides exacerbated by partition's legacy and territorial disputes such as Kashmir, underscoring causal links between demographic pressures, resource competition, and governance failures rather than sanitized narratives of harmonious pluralism.
